teacherNotes.note: Model disciplinary language aloud, teach annotation and source checking explicitly, use mixed-response modes, and give specific feedback on evidence, cohesion, viewpoint and vocabulary precision while increasing learner independence.

The AI tutor prompts in this unit assume an adult is present nearby whenever a learner practises with the device; remind families that children should not be left alone with it. Steer learners towards the tutor for the role-play interview, the vocabulary quizzes and the grammar checks, and ask them to bring recordings or written summaries to the live sessions so feedback stays grounded in real work.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Sample locations: 'havoc' in Imani's warning backstage, 'deft' in the description of Rohan's fingers, 'wallow' in the climax line 'The air wallowed in tension', 'meandered' in the holding-room scene and 'repugnant' in the confrontation. Accept any correct sentence copied from the story plus an original sentence that uses the word accurately.

Completed table: sabotage / sabotage / sabotaged; formidable pairs with formidably and has no everyday noun or verb; impulse / impulsive / impulsively; creation / create / creative / creatively; vulnerability / vulnerable / vulnerably; accuracy / accurate / accurately; materialisation / materialise / material / materially; repugnance / repugnant / repugnantly. Note that the source sheet printed the materialise row with its noun and verb columns swapped; mark against this corrected version.

Suggested pairs: aloof — distant / friendly; formidable — impressive / weak; vulnerable — exposed / protected; notorious — infamous / unknown; impulsive — spontaneous / deliberate; accurate — precise / inaccurate; repugnant — disgusting / pleasant. Accept any defensible alternatives.

Check each of the ten sentences keeps its word's meaning in a music or performance context, for example 'One broken cymbal caused havoc in the percussion section.' Reject sentences where the target word could be deleted without changing the meaning.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: A situation in which there is a lot of damage or confusion. The storm caused havoc in the town, knocking down trees and power lines.
Skilful and quick in movement or action. The deft musician played the oud beautifully, impressing everyone in the audience.
To make something become a certain way; to perform or deliver. The artist will render a beautiful painting for the school art show.
To gather together courage, strength, or support for a specific purpose. The teacher asked us to muster our courage and speak in front of the class.
To arrange or use something in a certain way for a purpose. The teacher decided to deploy new teaching methods to help students learn better.
havoc — Imani urges Rohan not to let the missing mask cause havoc, meaning damage and confusion, inside his head.
deft — the narrator contrasts Rohan's skilful, quick fingers with his calm face as he adjusts the costume collar.
render — in theatre terms, to render a theme is to perform it so clearly that the audience receives it.
Contortion — the play is titled The Last Contortion after the dancer's twisted, unnaturally bent body shapes.
notorious — Horizon East is well known for something negative: dramatic openings on stage and drama off it.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Music as Universal Language" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 12-13 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'havoc'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Explain what it means to call music a universal language and discuss how the performing arts connect people across cultures.
Read the story "The Curtain Never Lies" and answer comprehension and analysis questions using evidence from the text.
Use thirty key vocabulary words related to performance, creativity, emotion, and integrity in your own speaking and writing.
Form and use the Present Perfect Continuous tense correctly to describe actions that started in the past and are still continuing or have recently stopped.
Identify and create participle clauses to combine sentences and add detail in a more sophisticated way.
Use what clauses to form exclamatory sentences that express strong feelings or reactions.
Ask polite questions using appropriate structures such as "Could you...?", "Would you mind...?", and "Do you know...?"
Use reported speech to convey what someone else said without quoting their exact words.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "What Makes Music a Universal Language?" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Curtain Never Lies, Part 1: The Competition" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Present Perfect Continuous" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
